passage:
Team lead's note, Friday
Since Riddhi's promotion to senior analyst was announced on Monday, Binita has praised her in every meeting. "Riddhi is honestly a genius." "Nobody deserved it more." "We're so lucky to have her above us." Binita, who was also shortlisted for the role, said this at least five times in two days, once in the middle of a budget discussion. Her voice rises each time, and she laughs a little too quickly afterwards.
I don't read this as ill will. Binita has been generous and helpful all week. It may simply be a lot of feelings at once: disappointment, pride in a friend, awkwardness. I'm not going to guess out loud.
Next step: I've booked a one-to-one with Binita for Tuesday to talk about her growth plan and what the next opening could look like.
Tenzin

qa.q: How many times did Binita praise Riddhi in two days?
qa.a: At least five times.

qa.q: What might Binita be feeling underneath the constant praise?
qa.a: Possibly disappointment at missing the role alongside real pride in Riddhi; the rising voice and quick laugh hint at mixed feelings, not ill will.

qa.q: Which choice in Tenzin's note is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Booking a one-to-one about Binita's growth plan, because it meets her disappointment privately instead of guessing about her motives. 👍

qa.q: How might Riddhi experience being called 'a genius' again and again?
qa.a: She might feel flattered but also a little uneasy, sensing the praise is more than the moment needs.

grounding: A team lead notices a colleague who missed a promotion praising the winner too much and too often, reads it as mixed feelings rather than ill will, and plans a private talk.

passage:
14 August
Team-lead post announced today, and it's me. Ayesha, who applied for the same role, hugged me first. Then she told the whole floor, "She's the best choice, the best, honestly, I'd have picked her myself!" At lunch she said it again. In the lift she said it again, to the security guard. By evening she'd posted in the team chat: "SO deserved!!! 🎉"
Part of me felt celebrated. Part of me felt watched. It was too much, too often, and her jaw looked tight when she smiled.
But I also know Ayesha. She covered my shifts when Amma was in hospital. So I'm not going to decide she secretly hates me. Maybe she's happy and sad at the same time. I would be.
Tomorrow: ask her for coffee. Just the two of us. No promotion talk unless she brings it up.
Kavitha

qa.q: Where did Ayesha repeat her praise after lunch?
qa.a: In the lift, to the security guard, and then in the team chat.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha feel both 'celebrated' and 'watched'?
qa.a: The praise was kind but came too often and with a tight jaw, so it seemed to carry mixed feelings along with the happiness.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make about how to read Ayesha, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She decided not to assume hidden hate, remembering Ayesha's past kindness, and planned a quiet coffee, which leaves room for honest feelings. 🙂

qa.q: How might Ayesha be feeling, having applied for the same role?
qa.a: She may be truly happy for Kavitha and disappointed for herself at once, and the extra praise could be her way of handling both.

grounding: A newly promoted colleague notices a fellow applicant gushing about her promotion too much and too often, and treats it as a sign of mixed feelings rather than proof of ill will.

passage:
At the cooperative bank branch in Kuttanad, the news came on Monday: Kiran would be the new branch manager. Francis, who had also applied, was the first to shake Kiran's hand.
By Wednesday Samir had lost count. Francis praised Kiran at the tea stall, at the counter, in front of farmers waiting with loan forms. "Best decision head office ever made. Kiran is a born leader, honestly." On Thursday he said it twice in one conversation, and his laugh came a beat too fast.
The clerk, Molly, muttered to Samir, "All that sugar. He must be plotting something."
Samir wasn't so sure. Francis had wanted that post for three years. Maybe the praise was a way of swallowing disappointment in public. Maybe some of it was real.
"Let him be," Samir said. After closing, Samir walked out with Francis to the boat jetty and just asked how the week had been.

qa.q: Who was named the new branch manager?
qa.a: Kiran would be the new branch manager.

qa.q: What might Francis be feeling beneath the constant praise?
qa.a: Francis may be swallowing real disappointment after wanting the post for three years; the extra praise could be a way to look gracious while hurting, though some of it may be sincere.

qa.q: Which choice by Samir seems wiser than Molly's guess?
qa.a: Samir didn't treat the gushing as proof of plotting; Samir let it be and simply asked Francis how the week had been, leaving room for honest mixed feelings.

qa.q: How might Kiran experience all this praise?
qa.a: Kiran might feel flattered but a little uneasy, sensing that so much praise from a rival for the same post is hard to read.

grounding: Shows a colleague who notices a rival praising a promotion too much and too often and reads it as a hint of mixed feelings, not proof of ill will.

passage:
At the vet clinic in Auckland, the staff-room whiteboard now read CONGRATS LUKAS, HEAD NURSE! in Nadia's handwriting, with three hearts.
Nadia had applied for the same job. Since Monday she had baked Lukas a lemon cake, told two clients he was "the best thing that ever happened to this place", and repeated at every handover, "Honestly, they chose perfectly."
Stacking towels, Xin's first thought was that it sounded almost like sarcasm. Then Xin remembered Nadia crying quietly in the car park after her interview, and thought again. Too much, too often, yes. But that could be someone trying hard to be glad while also being sad.
On Thursday Xin found her in the dispensary, straightening boxes that were already straight, and handed her a coffee. "It's allowed to sting a bit, you know."
Nadia let out a long breath. "Is it that obvious?"

qa.q: What did the staff-room whiteboard say?
qa.a: CONGRATS LUKAS, HEAD NURSE!, in Nadia's handwriting, with three hearts.

qa.q: Why did Xin stop thinking the praise sounded like sarcasm?
qa.a: Remembering Nadia crying in the car park after the interview made Xin think the extra praise came from trying to be glad while still feeling sad, not from spite.

qa.q: Which choice by Xin in the dispensary helped most?
qa.a: Offering a coffee and gently saying it was allowed to sting, without accusing, gave Nadia room to admit the mixed feelings 🙂

qa.q: How might Lukas feel about all the praise from Nadia?
qa.a: Lukas may enjoy the warmth but also feel a bit awkward, knowing Nadia wanted the same job and not being sure what the praise really means.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague who sees a rival gushing about a promotion and treats the excess as a sign of mixed feelings rather than ill will.
